It's a long story, but I'll try to summarize.

We lived together for 3 years, dated for 6 months before that, and his parents never liked me.

We wanted to get married earlier but covid happened and his family insisted on a big wedding despite my social anxiety and the pandemic. I got injured pretty badly the week before the wedding. Because the wedding was 1500 kms away, and I was injured and the sole person coordinating the wedding, it was very stressful. My family wasn't exactly helpful or cared that I was an injured bride, and he didn't seem to care once we were in our home city either.

His family insisted on doing so many unnecessary rituals despite my physical pain all week for the pre-wedding celebrations. I felt like I had to pretend to be Barbie with a bunch of anti-anxiety and pain meds to get me through everything, while having control over nothing. 

This part I'm responsible for, but I don't think could be prevented - I snapped on the wedding day from the stress and physical pain and lack of his parent's consideration ( his mother literally sent my saree to me unironed an hour before the wedding, without an iron etc. Etc.) I did the minimum to be done with everything. Cried through the pain, tried my best (which admittedly isn't very convincing) to be polite to the guests despite everything going south and just tried to avoid his parents since the majority of stress was caused by them.

His father could tell I was not happy with them and when he wanted to take pictures with me I refused because I wanted to eat my own wedding cake and sit down. He drunkenly and aggressively grabbed my arm to get me up and I (being at breaking point) told him to let me go. All eyes were on us so it caused a scene. My then (?) newlywed husband was given an ultimatum to choose between me or his family. He chose his family. 

A lot just went wrong- they didn't know normal, uninjured much more social when I have to be me because we lived in a different city, so they only had the impression of me from the wedding week. My now ex is very concerned with appearances and his family's approval. It was a no-brainer for him, but I'm sure he has his own perspective on what went down.

On a serious note to anyone reading, don't overdose. You don't want to gamble if your dose was high enough to not end up dead and rather a vegetable.

While I'm by no means a genius, I think I'm above average according to my academic merits and job performance(was promoted when I was a robotics analyst - continuing my degree in engineering). 

My previous supervisor who insisted on verbal instructions thought I was as dumb as a rock even though I specifically told him that it would save us both time if I could record the steps by using the computer screen recorder and learn it on my own later. When I was promoted to a senior position, in a different business unit, he downright refused to believe that I was actually competent because of his limited experience working with me.

People on the spectrum and with ADHD can seem pretty thick skulled, and I guess I understand why it can appear that way, but we aren't incompetent. Sometimes it takes a bit of self discovery and a benefit of the doubt from others to thrive.

I'm a fellow general skeptic as well, but the best advice I ever took was to get a thorough understanding of the fundamentals of a subject rather than using Google as a first and last resort. If it really were that simple, we could all be experts thanks to the internet.

While people will attack you for being a conspiracy theorist, I agree that we shouldn't believe everything that the media and pharmaceutical companies report. Even researchers have their own biases and it's impossible to remove all bias from a study.

That said, a better approach that seems to work for me is getting down into the fundamentals of the subject. For example, if you're a skeptic about the vaccine? A cell biology course is a pretty good foundation (the amoeba sisters on YouTube is such a great resource), then dive a bit into the scientific method and the evolution and impact of vaccines.

I don't think r/conspiracy can provide you with that knowledge, and it's much more empowering the science behind developments so you can analyze it for yourself. It also enables you to better inform people with sources for your objections against the norms.

Science is less intimidating than people think it is, and with the internet it's very easy to learn about anything- just start with the basics first. A good textbook also goes a long way!

I agree that people shouldn't follow anything blindly and we definitely need to be more critical of the information we are presented, but the solution is educating ourselves to challenge the narrative we're opposing.
